title: The full sweep finishes under four minutes on a quiet machine: decisions are tested directly and real git is kept for the git contract
description: Owner decision 2026-10-30. P143.8 and P143.10 measured the sweep throughput-bound (about 2500 slot-seconds over 8 workers, 325-327 s quiet on darwin) with about 84% of the drive suite's time in process spawn; per-call git memoisation gave about 2% each and is exhausted. Most cases in tests/test_drive_phase.py, test_commit_task_work.py, test_audit_task.py and test_close_phase.py reach a decision through a real repository and real verbs although only the decision is under test. First measure: classify every case as decision-logic (git is scenery) or git-contract, with slot-seconds per class. Then convert the decision-logic cases suite by suite to call the pure decision functions on built state, keeping a small deliberate end-to-end set. Never re-record .github/sweep-costs.json from darwin.
desiredOutcome: python3 tools/sweep-selftests.py finishes under 240 s wall on the owner's machine, quiet, twice at least 20 minutes apart; every converted case still goes red on the defect it guards; the end-to-end set names what each case proves about git.

findings.issue: The guide's opening sentence 'Where a step branches on plain values, the branch is a planner under # --- deciding a step on facts ---' and the section comment's 'So each place a step branches on plain values is a planner here' claim more than the code does. Branches on plain values still decided inline: advance's file-return arm `if stored_green(...) != _evio.STORED_HOLDS` (drive-phase.py:4301), `if tree: integrate_member(...)` (4385), kept_tree_stop / redo_patch at the top of advance, writer_wait/writer_settle, triage's review_due / filed-at-head / owed_tasks branches ahead of the advance point, drive_locked's `pending['decision'] == 'triage'` and `pending.get('task')` note_sessions branches, and sign-off. A reader told every plain-value branch is a planner would look for one that does not exist.
findings.resolution: fixed in P152.13-6jb (025f279e51da): Narrow both sentences to what is true, e.g. 'Four of the drive's branch points are planners under ...: advance's writer/scope/reviewer/gate/risk/close, the triage's advance and tail, drive_locked's stale and route, and close_task's findings/lock/route/commit/answer; the other branches (the file-return arm's stored-green check, integrate_member, kept_tree_stop, the triage's head and owed checks, sign-off) are still decided inline.' Apply the same narrowing to the comment at drive-phase.py:3910-3912.

findings.issue: No case sends the sign-off-in-advance call through main() any more. The removed sq2 was an end-to-end drive: file a clean phase review, send `next P1 --answer sign-off --reason ...`, and assert exit 0, `done`, exactly one signoff verb call, and the signedOff/landed/released did-line. sq1 is still a drive and still asserts that the dispatch PRINTS that call, but nothing sends it. sq0, sq2, sq3, sq4, sq5, sq3m and sq0m now only ask the predicates and planners: `_pending_turn('route')`, `_triage_plan('advance')`, `advance_applies`, plus `apply_phase_answer` called directly. The wiring that acts on their answer goes unexercised: route 'advance' sets ctx['advance'], drive_phase carries it to the triage point, `if sent == "advance"` applies it, and `if sent == "not-applied"` prints the triage. Read, not run: a mutation of drive-phase.py:7563 to `if reason is not None:` (apply whenever an advance was sent, ignoring the planner) would leave every remaining case green, because no kept drive sends an advance. This is the path the phase-review dispatch tells the main loop to take for every clean phase, and its one-call sign-off is the cost property sq2 pinned. findings.issue: Children can go untraced without anything noticing, and it happens in the suite this tool is built for. The hook reaches a child only as the FIRST `sitecustomize` on PYTHONPATH. tests/test_drive_phase.py's `_pinned_clock` (line 286) and `_windows_stdout` (line 313) put a fixture directory holding its own `sitecustomize.py` ahead of it. Python imports only one `sitecustomize`, and the fixture's does not chain, so every drive-phase.py verb child started inside those blocks runs untraced at BOTH revisions. Those verbs are the stamped and CRLF routes: `_pinned_clock(` appears 5 times and `_windows_stdout(` twice, at both 92c399f5 and HEAD. The tool cannot detect this. The empty-reach refusal is per revision (line 522), and the printed `processes traced` counts only processes that dumped (read_traces, line 363). A child that never ran the hook, or ran it and ended through os._exit or a kill, is in no number. The counts also cannot separate 'fewer processes because drives were converted', which is the expected effect of the conversions this tool gates, from 'processes untraced'. A conversion at P152.4, P152.11 or P152.13 that drops a pinned-clock drive loses lines that were never in the base reach, and the tool exits 0. The docstring lists 'another sitecustomize earlier on its path' generically, but neither the docstring nor the filed outcome says that the target suite has that shape.
findings.resolution: fixed in P152.14-6jb (71166ef3aecf): Also write the hook as `usercustomize.py` in the same directory, guarded so it installs once per process. site.py imports usercustomize independently of which sitecustomize won wherever user site is enabled; say where it is not (-s, PYTHONNOUSERSITE, a venv without system site). Have the hook write a start marker when it installs. read_traces then prints started against dumped per revision, which makes os._exit and kills visible, plus a count of processes reached only through the usercustomize entry, which makes shadowing visible. Add a selftest case whose fixture suite starts the module's child under a non-chaining `sitecustomize` planted first on PYTHONPATH, and assert that the child's lines are measured. Prove it red against the current single entry point.

findings.file: tools/reach-diff.py:252-253,533 (gone excluded from the exit code); docstring 46-52
findings.issue: contradicts task clause 'prints every line reached at the base revision and not reached at the head revision ... exit 1 when any such line exists and 0 otherwise'. A base-reached line whose (function, text, occurrence) key the head module no longer holds is listed as `gone` and never decides the exit code (`result["code"] = 1 if found["gaps"] else 0`). So when a conversion renames a function, or extracts a planner and moves lines out of a route function, every moved line the head suite no longer reaches leaves the exit code 0. Its text can still be in the module, unreached. The gates P152.4, P152.11 and P152.13 read the exit code, so this is a pass that measured a loss. rd16 pins the reworded-and-still-reached case. No case covers moved-to-another-function-and-unreached.
findings.resolution: fixed in P152.14-6jb (71166ef3aecf): Before declaring a key gone, match it again by (stripped text, occurrence in the whole module) at the head. A match the head did not reach is a gap, which exits 1. Only text the head module no longer holds anywhere stays `gone`. Add a fixture tag that moves `return "positive"` into a renamed helper and drops its case, and assert exit 1. Alternatively, if `gone` is meant to stay non-deciding, amend the task description and the CONTRIBUTING bullet to say so. The current code does not do what the clause asked.

findings.issue: A lost line can hide behind an identical line in the same function whenever the module changes in that function, and this is neither documented nor tested. `occurrence` counts the earlier identical lines in the function. Inserting or removing one identical line above (`return 0`, `return code`, `continue`; the short route lines this tool exists to keep reached) shifts every later occurrence. Example: base f reaches A=`return 0` (occ0) and B=`return 0` (occ1). The head adds N=`return 0` above both, so N is occ0, A is occ1 and B is occ2, and the head reaches N and A. Base occ0 matches N and base occ1 matches A, both reached. B's loss is hidden and the exit is 0. When the module is byte-identical, as drive-phase.py was in the executor's real run, keys coincide and nothing hides. A conversion that also edits the module is exposed. rd10 proves only that two occurrences are distinct keys, not that an insertion leaves them stable.
findings.resolution: fixed in P152.14-6jb (71166ef3aecf): Align the base and head lines of each function with difflib.SequenceMatcher over stripped text instead of an occurrence index, so an inserted or deleted duplicate does not renumber the others. Add a fixture tag that inserts an identical earlier line and drops reach to the later one, and assert exit 1 naming it. At minimum, state the limitation in the docstring's matching section.

findings.issue: The bullet says the tool 'exits 1 naming each line of the module reached before and not after' and that the tracer runs 'in every Python process the suite starts'. Both overclaim. findings.resolution: fixed in P152.14-6jb (71166ef3aecf): Say that lines whose function or text changed are listed apart as gone and do not fail it, unless finding 2 is fixed. findings.issue: The tool changes the route of the run it measures. Its hook directory holds a `sitecustomize.py` on PYTHONPATH, and `_needs_process()` returns True for any PYTHONPATH entry holding one. Under reach-diff, every verb tests/test_drive_phase.py would run in-process therefore runs as a process: that accounts for the thousands of traced processes and the 717 s wall in the real run. drive-phase.py's real `run_verb` subprocess route is then reached because of the tool, not the suite. The effect is the same at both revisions, so it creates no false gap while the routing stays the same. It is still a measured reach that differs from what the sweep runs, and nothing says so.
findings.resolution: fixed in P152.14-6jb (71166ef3aecf): The usercustomize entry from finding 1 also removes this, because the detector looks only for sitecustomize.py. Otherwise, name this effect in the docstring's WHAT IT CANNOT SEE section.

findings.issue: sr16's check `code != M.E_PROVED and block.get("status") != "proved"` is satisfied by _judged's record refusal, which returns `(None, {"record": ...})`: None != E_PROVED and an absent redFirst has no status. So if `_wants_second` started owing a second run for a SyntaxError under --introduces (part of what sr16 guards: syntax errors never qualify), _judged refuses the record and sr16 stays green. _judged's docstring says 'the exit is None, `record` says which run, and the case reading it fails', which is not true for a case whose check is phrased as a negation. Today sr16 gets exit 3 from both the judged run and the real one (see note), so this is a latent hole, not a present wrong verdict.
findings.resolution: Make _judged raise (for example AssertionError naming the key and the run) on a record mismatch instead of returning None, so the refusal fails the enclosing block under its name however the case's check is worded. At the least, tighten sr16 to `code == M.E_CANNOT_PROVE and block.get("status") == "could-not-prove"`.

findings.issue: A comparison whose two sides materialise the same tree exits 0 with no change measured. The new WORKTREE head makes this the likely failure: `--base HEAD --head WORKTREE` on a clean checkout, or after the task's work is committed (when a phase review re-runs a task gate), copies exactly the base commit and reports 'lost: 0 lines'. The same happens with `--base X --head X`. The task exists because a gate passed vacuously (`--head HEAD` over an uncommitted conversion compares the base with itself). The diff fixes that spelling and leaves the same vacuous pass open under the new one. P152.4's re-pointed gate in the working tree's plan is now spelled exactly `--base HEAD --head WORKTREE`.
findings.resolution: In compare(), after both sides are prepared, refuse with 2 when they hold the same content. Either the two sides resolve to the same commit, or the head is WORKTREE and the scratch copy is byte-identical to the base export. Comparing the two scratch trees touches no git state. Print it as 'the head is the base: no change to measure'. Add a selftest case: `--base HEAD --head WORKTREE` over a clean fixture checkout exits 2.

findings.issue: A blind spot is matched only by the number of untraced children per block label. The docstring says such a block 'measured the same blind spot on both sides', and CONTRIBUTING says 'the same such children'. Equal counts do not establish that. Suppose the base kills a child that runs path P (P reached nowhere else) and the head kills a different child in the same block. The counts match, P's loss is invisible, and the run exits 0. In a suite with no STAGES table the label is '(whole file)', so the match is one count over the whole suite. The residual risk is half-stated ('lines only those children ran are measured at neither revision'), but the sentence before it claims identity.
findings.resolution: Record each module child's identity: the child dumps its argv with the export root stripped, and the parent's `spawned` records the same key. Then match the multiset of untraced keys per block instead of their count. If identity matching is not wanted, reword the docstring and the CONTRIBUTING sentence to say the same NUMBER of children, and state that a different child killed at the head hides a loss among the lines the base's child ran.

findings.issue: The hook reads the block label in the atexit handler (`os.environ.get("REACH_DIFF_BLOCK")` inside dump()), not when it installs. A suite process that clears or replaces os.environ before exiting has its untraced children filed under '(whole file)'. In a staged run that label ran at neither side, so the run refuses with 2 and names the wrong block. This fails safe, but the refusal is misattributed. `parent` is already captured at install time.
findings.resolution: Capture `block = os.environ.get("REACH_DIFF_BLOCK")` beside `parent` in _reach_diff_install() and write that value in dump().

findings.issue: The three converted callers (lv_call, gs_gate, _cli_here) call run_script_in_process with no process fallback, and the runner now raises ValueError when the environment's PYTHONPATH holds a sitecustomize. reach-diff puts one there by design. When the interpreter's user site is off (-s, PYTHONNOUSERSITE, or any venv without system site packages), it writes its hook as sitecustomize rather than usercustomize (tools/reach-diff.py:41-44, 55-57, 767). Under it every in-process fb, at4 and at6 call in test_audit_task raises, because _cli_here and lv_env copy os.environ (PYTHONPATH included) and gs_gate inherits it. The suite is then green at base HEAD (processes) and red at WORKTREE, so this task's own declared gate `reach-diff.py ... --head WORKTREE` cannot pass on such an interpreter. test_drive_phase avoids this only because it routes through _needs_process before calling the runner. The PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE sentence 'it refuses an env planting a sitecustomize ... so a case whose subject is the process boundary still starts one' is false for these callers: nothing starts a process, the case raises.
findings.resolution: fixed in P152.17-6jb (5bb44004d1a1): Route the way the drive suite does. outcome.technical: New tools/reach-diff.py: `python3 tools/reach-diff.py <module> <suite> --base <rev> --head <rev> [--repo PATH] [--jobs N] [--timeout S] [--tracer monitoring|settrace]`. Exit 0 when no line is lost, 1 when one is, 2 on a usage error or when no comparison could be made. It never writes the checkout. Each revision is a `git archive` export streamed through tarfile into a mkdtemp scratch, removed in `finally` through _suite.remove_tree. The suite runs through the sweep's own run_one and grade, loaded with _loader.load as prove-gates does, so children get the sweep's cwd, TMPDIR, HOME, git config and session-variable filtering. There is one job per STAGES block (`--selftest --stage LABEL`), or one whole-file run when sweep.is_staged or sweep.stage_labels say no. Both revisions' jobs share one ThreadPoolExecutor of sweep.default_jobs() workers; the default timeout is twice the sweep's DEFAULT_TIMEOUT. The tracer is a sitecustomize module written to a scratch directory that is put first on PYTHONPATH, so it runs in every Python process the suite starts, children included.
